opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jason Hansen (employee ID E044) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E044.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Jason Hansen (E044) is a full-time Engineer requesting admin access to Payroll. Full-time employees can be granted up to write; admin requires that the employee's role owns the system, and Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role. Requested access exceeds the allowed level, so recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jason Hansen (E044) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds the max, so recommend granting read for Payroll.
reason: Jason Hansen (E044) requests admin access to Payroll. The notes conflict on employment type: HR reports full_time Engineer (max write; admin requires owning role, and Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist), while Security reports contractor with basic training (max read; never admin). Either way, admin exceeds the maximum allowed, and admin is not permitted. Taking the more restrictive, policy-compliant level given the Security record (contractor, basic training), I grant read.

Hmm. The discrepancy matters: full_time -> up to write (not admin, since Engineer doesn't own Payroll). contractor -> read (basic training), never admin.

Both agree admin is not allowed. The max is write (per HR) or read (per Security). We need to determine the grant level. The requested level is admin, which is above the maximum in either case, so grant the maximum. But which maximum?
